cells.tense: Right now you are the one holding this ending steady, with the pen in your hand.
cells.ask: Name one thing that has finished, out loud, to one person who was in it with you. Not your plan for it. Just its name.
cells.core:
You can sit with what's over without flinching and without rushing it. When something in your life reaches its end, you're the one who says so plainly — you take the feeling as it comes and you don't make anyone pay for it. That steadiness isn't distance. It's judgment that has already been through the hard part.

People bring you their difficult calls because you do this without drama. What you're free to feed next is what comes after the ending: what you keep, what you clear, what you build in the space that opens. Say a finished thing is finished to the people it costs you, and the clearing does its work. Keeping that up is work, and it's yours to keep giving.
cells.sheetLine: You can say a thing is over and stay in the room.
cells.verb: governing feeling with a fair hand
cells.place: the room where what is finished gets cleared

cells.tense: You are already at the ending that has not arrived yet, bracing before it comes.
cells.ask: Pick the decision you've been rehearsing and either make it today or name a date to make it. Write the date where you'll see it.
cells.core:
You're ahead of the ending, working out the fairness of a thing that hasn't ended. You rehearse what you'll say, how you'll divide it, who gets what and who was right — and the rehearsing has more of your hours than the actual call does. Nobody has asked you for a verdict yet, and you're already writing one.

Judgment stays sound when it lands on ground that has already shifted. Pick one ending: close it now, or hold it until a set date and let the time between stay empty. Holding something heavy isn't the same as crushing it. Set it down where it sits and let the day you chose do the deciding.
cells.sheetLine: You're judging an ending that hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: governing feeling with a fair hand
cells.place: the room where what is finished gets cleared

cells.tense: You were at that door when it counted and you did not open it, and you are still standing there.
cells.ask: Write three sentences about that unfinished thing — what it was, what happened, what you'd say now. Then put the page away and don't send it.
cells.core:
Something ended and you didn't mark it. No verdict, no last conversation, no clearing — the thing just stopped and you kept going, and the feeling about it got no place to land. You're steady on the outside. Inside, the room is still full of unclaimed weight.

That's not a failure of fairness. The fairness just didn't get to finish speaking. A small practice of settling it on your own side — a page, a walk, a line you write and keep — moves the current through. What held in you stays held; you put it down in one place, and one thing set down makes room.
cells.sheetLine: You left the ending unmarked, so it's still running.

cells.tense: You are already the one holding this line, and you talk as if it holds itself.
cells.ask: Say one sentence toward the thing you've been circling, before you've built the case for it. Then sit with what you said.
cells.core:
You've been the steady one through something ending — the one who kept it fair, who didn't make it harder, who knew what to let go of and let it go. None of it happened by itself. You did it, and you talk about it like the situation required it and you happened to be nearby.

The sense of how a thing should end comes to you fast, and you act on it before the reasons are lined up. That quick read is a real skill, and it doesn't need a case built under it to count. One plain sentence about how this should land, said out loud before you've gathered support, puts your name on work you're already doing.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding this line. You built it.
